summary.text: The acid dissociation constant, Ka, describes how far an acid HA splits into its conjugate base A⁻ and a hydrogen ion H⁺ at equilibrium.
pKₐ is a logarithmic form of Ka, and a lower pKₐ means a stronger acid, while acetic acid has a pKₐ of 4.7.
With concentrations, pKₐ values let chemists predict a solution's pH, and they are needed to prepare buffer solutions.

facts.label: Pauling's rules
facts.value: One for polyprotic acids, one for oxyacids

items.prompt: At equilibrium, acid P is less dissociated than acid Q. Which statement is right?

options.label: Acid P has the lower Ka and is the weaker acid
Acid P has the higher Ka and is the stronger acid
Acid P has the lower Ka and is the stronger acid
The two acids must have the same Ka

items.explain: A lower Ka corresponds to a weaker acid, meaning one that is less dissociated at equilibrium.

items.prompt: Acid X has a pKₐ of 3 and acid Y has a pKₐ of 5. Which is the stronger acid?

options.label: Acid Y, because a higher pKₐ means a stronger acid
Acid X, because a lower pKₐ means a stronger acid
Acid X, because a lower pKₐ means a weaker acid
Neither, because pKₐ says nothing about strength

items.explain: A lower pKₐ corresponds to a stronger acid.

items.prompt: A reaction that absorbs heat is warmed up. What happens to the Ka of that dissociation?

options.label: It decreases
It stays the same, since Ka is fixed for an acid
It drops to zero
It increases

items.explain: For an endothermic reaction Ka increases and pKₐ decreases as temperature rises, which follows from Le Chatelier's principle.

items.prompt: When an acid HA dissociates in solution, which two species appear?

options.label: The conjugate base A⁻ and a hydrogen ion H⁺
A salt and some water
A metal and hydrogen gas
A hydroxide ion and the original acid

items.explain: The acid HA dissociates into its conjugate base A⁻ and a hydrogen ion H⁺.

items.prompt: A weak acid solution has sat until its concentrations stopped changing. What is going on at the molecular level?

options.label: All reactions have stopped completely
Only the forward reaction continues until the acid is gone
Forward and backward reactions both continue at the same rate
Only the backward reaction continues

items.explain: Equilibrium means the concentrations do not change over time because the forward and backward reactions occur at the same rate.

items.prompt: Many medicines are weak acids or bases. What can a drug's pKₐ help chemists estimate?

options.label: How cheaply a tablet can be made
How far the compound enters the bloodstream
How quickly a tablet crumbles on a shelf
How sweet the medicine tastes

items.explain: Knowing the pKₐ, together with the octanol-water partition coefficient, can be used to estimate the extent to which a compound enters the blood stream.

paragraphs.heading: An acid coming apart
paragraphs.text: When an acid, written HA, is in solution, some of it splits into A⁻ and a hydrogen ion, H⁺. In acid–base chemistry this splitting is called dissociation, and A⁻ is called the conjugate base of the acid. The splitting and the rejoining both keep going, and once they run at the same rate the amounts stop changing; that steady state is equilibrium. For acids, chemists describe it with an equilibrium constant called the acid dissociation constant, written Kₐ.

paragraphs.heading: Ka and pKa
paragraphs.text: A lower Kₐ means a weaker acid, one that has split apart less at equilibrium. Chemists often use pKₐ instead, because it gives a convenient logarithmic scale. For a made-up weak acid with Kₐ = 10⁻⁵, log Kₐ is −5, so pKₐ = 5. Acetic acid has Kₐ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ and a pKₐ of 4.7. On this scale the direction flips: a lower pKₐ means a stronger acid.

paragraphs.heading: What sets the value
paragraphs.text: Kₐ follows directly from the thermodynamics of the dissociation, and pKₐ is directly proportional to the reaction's standard Gibbs free energy change. It also shifts with temperature, in a way Le Chatelier's principle explains. For an endothermic dissociation, warming raises Kₐ and lowers pKₐ; for an exothermic one, the reverse holds. The acid's molecular structure matters too, through inductive effects, mesomeric effects and hydrogen bonding.

paragraphs.heading: Predicting pH
paragraphs.text: You can only understand how acids and bases behave in solution, in numbers, if you know their pKₐ values. If you know the concentrations and pKₐ values of every acid and base present, you can predict the solution's pH. Going the other way, if you know the pH, you can work out how much of each acid and base is there at equilibrium. These calculations are used across chemistry, biology, medicine and geology, and pKₐ values are needed to prepare buffer solutions.

paragraphs.heading: From medicine to the ocean
paragraphs.text: Many medicines are weak acids or bases. Their pKₐ values, together with a measure called the octanol-water partition coefficient, help estimate how much of a drug gets into the bloodstream. Acidity plays a basic role in natural waters, so these constants are essential in aquatic chemistry and chemical oceanography. In living things, keeping acid–base balance and the speed of enzyme reactions both rely on the pKₐ values of all the different acids and bases found in cells and in the body.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring it
paragraphs.text: In the lab, pKₐ can be measured with a pH titration. For very low values, below about 2, or very high ones, above about 11, pH readings become hard to make in practice. In those cases spectrophotometric or NMR measurements may be needed instead.
